meta.name: Pneumonia — Mild Hypoxia, Supportive BLS Care

patient.name: Eleanor Voss
patient.chiefComplaint: Productive cough, fever, and feeling weak and short of breath for two days

history.hpi: Daughter reports patient has had a productive cough with yellow-green sputum, subjective fevers, and chills for two days, now with increasing fatigue and mild shortness of breath, worse with exertion. No chest pain. No known sick contacts. Patient lives alone and daughter checked in after she didn't answer the phone this morning.
history.lastOralIntake: Tea and toast this morning, poor appetite for two days
history.events: Daughter arrived to check on patient and found her tired-appearing and short of breath, called 911

scene.location: Single-story home, patient seated in living room recliner
scene.bystanders: Daughter present, called 911 after finding patient unwell
visualCues: Patient seated upright in recliner, mild work of breathing
Frequent productive cough into a tissue, sputum yellow-green
Empty water glass and untouched plate of food nearby

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 74-year-old female seated upright in a recliner, tired-appearing, with a frequent productive cough and mild increased work of breathing.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in full sentences with occasional pauses to cough
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Mildly increased work of breathing, productive cough, diminished breath sounds with crackles at the right lower lobe
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and flushed
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities, appears fatigued
otherFindings: Frequent productive cough with yellow-green sputum
Subjective fever/chills reported over past two days
Mild accessory muscle use with exertion
Poor oral intake for two days
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I just feel so tired... and this cough won't quit."

transitions.condition: Crew promptly assesses full vital signs and breath sounds, applies supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula titrated to target saturation, and positions the patient upright for comfort.
Crew focuses on history-taking and packaging without promptly applying supplemental oxygen, allowing hypoxia to worsen.

phases.name: Oxygen and positioning provided
phases.description: Crew applies supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula titrated to target saturation, keeps the patient in a position of comfort, and continues monitoring while preparing for transport.
phases.triggerCondition: After the crew completes a full set of vital signs and breath sound assessment, they promptly apply nasal cannula oxygen titrated toward the 94–98% target and maintain the patient in an upright position of comfort.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improved work of breathing, still productive cough, crackles persist at right lower lobe
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm
otherFindings: Nasal cannula in place at 2 L/min
Positioned upright in position of comfort
Speaking in fuller sentences with less pausing
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That does feel a little easier, thank you."

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess full vital signs, breath sounds, and mental status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Exam: Full set of vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment), temperature, and O2 saturation... Breath sounds (wheezes, crackles, rales, rhonchi, diminished, clear)... Mental status (alert, tired, lethargic, unresponsive)
expectedActions.rationale: Establishes baseline severity and guides oxygen titration and transport priority.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply nasal cannula O2 titrated to 94–98% SpO2
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Give supplemental oxygen for dyspnea to a target of 94–98% saturation. Escalate from a nasal cannula as needed to reach this goal
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects hypoxia from pneumonia-related V/Q mismatch.

expectedActions.shortAction: Position patient upright in position of comfort
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient positioning can significantly impact respiratory mechanics... Elevating the head or padding (shoulders, occiput) can assist with opening airway and respiratory mechanics. This can both improve the ability to ventilate and limit aspiration
expectedActions.rationale: Upright positioning eases work of breathing and reduces aspiration risk.

expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pulse oximetry and EtCO2 should be routinely used as adjuncts to other forms of monitoring in patients with respiratory complaints
expectedActions.rationale: Continuous monitoring detects trending desaturation before clinical decompensation is obvious.

transitions.condition: Oxygenation and comfort have improved with nasal cannula O2 and positioning; patient is packaged for transport with ongoing reassessment.

phases.name: Reassessed and prepared for transport
phases.description: Patient's oxygenation and comfort have improved with supplemental oxygen and positioning; crew continues serial reassessment and supportive care en route.
phases.triggerCondition: After oxygen and positioning are in place and the patient shows improved saturation and reduced work of breathing, the crew packages her for transport with ongoing reassessment.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and pink
otherFindings: Nasal cannula O2 in place, saturations improved
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel a bit better now, thank you for taking care of me."

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs and response to oxygen/positioning en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Percentage of patients with abnormal pulse oximetry, respiratory rate, EtCO2 value with normalization on final set of vital signs
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms the patient continues to respond to supportive care and detects any deterioration early.

phases.name: Oxygen delayed
phases.description: Without prompt supplemental oxygen, the patient's hypoxia and work of breathing worsen, with increasing accessory muscle use and anxiety.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew delays applying supplemental oxygen while focusing on history-taking, allowing hypoxia to progress and work of breathing to increase.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Increased work of breathing, accessory muscle use, more frequent coughing
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities, appears increasingly anxious
otherFindings: Patient appears more anxious and fatigued

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize worsening hypoxia; apply O2 titrated to 94–98% SpO2 without further delay
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Give supplemental oxygen for dyspnea to a target of 94–98% saturation. Escalate from a nasal cannula as needed to reach this goal
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed oxygen allows preventable hypoxia to progress; prompt correction reverses the trend.
